solution:
Soft iron is a SOFT ferromagnetic material: it has a very large permeability \((\mu_{r} > 1000)\) together with very small retentivity and coercivity, i.e. a narrow hysteresis loop.

Why each half of that matters for an electromagnet:
(a) The large permeability is what does the work. A soft iron rod placed in the core of a solenoid multiplies the field of the solenoid about a thousand-fold, because \(B = \mu_{0}\mu_{r}H\) and the same current \(H = nI\) then produces a far larger \(B\).
(b) The small retentivity is what makes it an ELECTROMAGNET rather than a permanent magnet. When the current is switched off, \(H = 0\); because soft iron retains almost no magnetisation, the field effectively falls to zero and the magnet 'lets go'. A material with high retentivity would stay magnetised and could not be switched off.

So the useful property is: high permeability with low retentivity (and low coercivity), so the magnetism can be created strongly and removed completely by the current.

Ferromagnetism depends on the exchange coupling between neighbouring magnetic dipole moments, which is what holds all the moments in a domain parallel to one another. As the temperature is raised, thermal agitation distorts the domain structure and weakens that coupling.

At a definite temperature, called the CURIE TEMPERATURE \(T_{C}\) of the material, the domain structure collapses completely. Above \(T_{C}\) the material is no longer ferromagnetic — it behaves like a PARAMAGNETIC material: the atoms still carry magnetic dipole moments, but these are now randomly oriented by thermal motion instead of being locked parallel, so the strong spontaneous magnetisation, the hysteresis and the ability to become a permanent magnet are all lost.

Above the Curie point the susceptibility follows the Curie-Weiss form
\(\chi = \dfrac{C}{T - T_{C}}\) for \(T > T_{C}\) --- Eq. (11.22),
so \(\chi\) falls off as the temperature is raised further. (For metallic iron \(T_{C} = 1043\) K, for metallic nickel 631 K.)

A permanent magnet must stay strongly magnetised with NO current and no external field maintaining it, and it must not be demagnetised easily by handling, heating or a stray opposing field. Reading those two requirements off the hysteresis loop:

(a) RETENTIVITY must be HIGH. Retentivity is the value of \(B\) that survives when \(H\) is brought back to zero (point b of Fig. 11.11). It is exactly the strength the magnet keeps after the magnetising current is switched off, so it must be as large as possible.

(b) COERCIVITY must be HIGH. Coercivity is the reverse magnetising field needed to bring \(B\) back to zero (point c of Fig. 11.11). A large coercivity means a large opposing field is required to destroy the magnetisation, i.e. the magnet resists being demagnetised.

Both requirements together mean a WIDE hysteresis loop, which is the loop of a HARD ferromagnetic material such as steel or alnico — the opposite of the narrow loop of the soft iron used for electromagnets and transformer cores.

Curie's law (Pierre Curie, 1895) applies to a PARAMAGNETIC material. Its atoms each carry a permanent magnetic dipole moment, but thermal agitation keeps these moments randomly oriented, so the net magnetisation is zero until a field is applied. An applied field tries to align the moments (alignment lowers the potential energy \(U = -mB\cos\theta\)) while thermal energy tries to randomise them, so the degree of alignment rises with \(B\) and falls with temperature.

Statement: the magnetisation \(M\) of a paramagnetic material is directly proportional to the applied magnetic field \(B\) and inversely proportional to its absolute temperature \(T\):
\(M = C\dfrac{B}{T}\) --- Eq. (11.20),
where \(C\) is the Curie constant of the material.

Writing \(B = \mu_{0}H\) and using \(\chi = M/H\) (Eq. 11.17):
\(M = C\dfrac{\mu_{0}H}{T}\), so \(\chi = \mu_{r} - 1 = C\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{T}\), i.e. \(\chi \propto \dfrac{1}{T}\) --- Eq. (11.21).

Consequence: increasing the applied field and lowering the temperature both align more moments and so increase the magnetisation. The law holds only while the material is paramagnetic and \(H\) is not so strong that saturation is approached; above the Curie point a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic and obeys the modified form \(\chi = C/(T - T_{C})\).

Consider an electron of charge \(e\) moving with constant speed \(v\) in a circular orbit of radius \(r\) about the nucleus. A revolving charge is equivalent to a tiny current loop, so it has a magnetic dipole moment.

Step 1 - the equivalent current. The electron covers the circumference \(2\pi r\) in one period \(T\), so \(v = 2\pi r/T\), i.e. \(T = 2\pi r/v = 2\pi/\omega\). The charge crossing any point of the orbit per unit time is
\(I = \dfrac{e}{T} = \dfrac{e\omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}\) --- Eq. (11.9).

Step 2 - the dipole moment of that loop. For a current loop, \(m = IA\), and here \(A = \pi r^{2}\):
\(m_{orb} = IA = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r} \times \pi r^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}evr\) --- Eq. (11.10).

Step 3 - in terms of angular momentum. The orbital angular momentum of the electron is \(L = m_{e}vr\), so
\(m_{orb} = \left(\dfrac{e}{2m_{e}}\right)(m_{e}vr) = \left(\dfrac{e}{2m_{e}}\right)L\) --- Eq. (11.11).
The orbital magnetic moment is thus proportional to the angular momentum; the constant \(e/2m_{e}\) is called the GYROMAGNETIC RATIO. Because the electron's charge is negative, \(\vec{m}_{orb}\) is directed OPPOSITE to \(\vec{L}\):
\(\vec{m}_{orb} = -\dfrac{e}{2m_{e}}\vec{L}\).

Step 4 - quantisation. Bohr's second postulate gives \(L = m_{e}vr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\), so
\(m_{orb} = \dfrac{enh}{4\pi m_{e}}\).
For the first orbit \((n = 1)\), \(m_{orb} = \dfrac{eh}{4\pi m_{e}}\), which is called the BOHR MAGNETON and has the value \(9.274 \times 10^{-24}\) A m\(^{2}\).

The hysteresis loop is the closed \(B\)-\(H\) curve obtained when a ferromagnetic sample is carried through one complete cycle of magnetisation (Fig. 11.11). What it represents:

(a) It represents the MAGNETIC HISTORY of the sample. The return path never retraces the outward path, so \(B\) is not a single-valued function of \(H\) — the value of \(B\) depends on what the specimen has been through before. This lagging of \(B\) behind \(H\) is what the word hysteresis means.

(b) It displays the four characteristic quantities of the material: SATURATION (point a, where all domains have merged and further \(H\) produces no further \(B\)); RETENTIVITY or remanence (point b, the \(B\) left when \(H = 0\)); COERCIVITY (point c, the reverse \(H\) needed to bring \(B\) to zero); and the same pair again in the reverse sense (points d, e).

(c) Its AREA represents the energy dissipated as heat, per unit volume of the material, in taking it once round the cycle — the work done in repeatedly reorienting the domains, which is not recovered. This is the direct analogue of the stress-strain hysteresis of Std XI, where the area inside the loop is the energy lost in deforming the material.

It is therefore also the practical basis for choosing a material: a narrow loop (small area, small coercivity and retentivity) means a soft material suited to transformer cores and electromagnets, and a wide loop means a hard material suited to permanent magnets.

Application: the giant lifting electromagnet used on a crane in a scrap yard or steel plant.

How it works. A coil of many turns is wound on a core of soft iron and a large direct current is passed through it. The field of the solenoid alone is \(B_{0} = \mu_{0}nI\); with the soft iron core it becomes \(B = \mu_{0}\mu_{r}nI\), and since soft iron has \(\mu_{r} > 1000\) the field is increased about a thousand-fold. The crane can then pick up very heavy iron and steel loads that no ordinary magnet could hold.

Why soft iron is the right core here. When the load is to be released, the current is simply switched off. Because soft iron has very low retentivity, its magnetisation almost vanishes with the current and the load drops. A material with high retentivity would keep the load stuck to the magnet.

Other applications mentioned in the chapter are electric bells, loud speakers and circuit breakers, and superconducting electromagnets producing fields of a few tesla for research and for NMR (Nuclear Magnetic Resonance) spectroscopy.
